name: Chronic actinic dermatitis
aliases: photosensitivity dermatitis and actinic reticuloid syndrome

clinicalPearls: A persistent, eczematous photosensitivity seen predominantly in older men, in whom it can be severe and disabling

Chronic, itchy, lichenified and sometimes infiltrated plaques develop on sun-exposed skin, with a sharp cut-off at clothing lines and sparing of shaded areas such as behind the ears and under the chin
In its most florid form (actinic reticuloid) the skin becomes thickened and leonine, which can mimic cutaneous lymphoma both clinically and histologically
Phototesting characteristically shows a markedly reduced threshold to ultraviolet B, usually extending to ultraviolet A and sometimes into visible light
There is a frequent association with contact and photocontact allergy, for example to fragrances, plants (Compositae) and sunscreen chemicals, which should be sought by patch and photopatch testing
Rigorous photoprotection with clothing and broad-spectrum sunscreen is essential, alongside avoidance of identified contact allergens and treatment of the dermatitis
Topical and systemic immunosuppression is used for resistant disease, and low-dose desensitisation phototherapy may help selected patients
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic actinic dermatitis is thought to arise as a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction in which ultraviolet radiation modifies an endogenous cutaneous protein to create a persistent photoantigen, driving an ongoing eczematous, T-cell mediated inflammatory response in light-exposed skin. Many patients have coexisting contact or photocontact allergies, and it is proposed that longstanding allergic contact dermatitis can evolve into a self-perpetuating photosensitive state. In the actinic reticuloid variant the dense dermal lymphocytic infiltrate can resemble cutaneous T-cell lymphoma histologically, although the process is benign and reactive.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides / Sezary syndrome)
Airborne allergic contact dermatitis (for example to Compositae plants)
Photoallergic contact dermatitis or drug photosensitivity
Atopic or seborrhoeic dermatitis of the head and neck
additionalInvestigations: Phototesting demonstrating a reduced minimal erythema dose, usually to ultraviolet B and ultraviolet A
Patch and photopatch testing to identify contact and photocontact allergens
Skin biopsy to characterise the dermatitis and, in actinic reticuloid, to distinguish it from cutaneous lymphoma
Peripheral blood film and lymphocyte studies where lymphoma is a concern
Antinuclear antibody testing to exclude lupus erythematosus
Review of medications and topical products that may contribute to photosensitivity
redFlags: Leonine facies or erythroderma raising the possibility of underlying cutaneous lymphoma
Circulating atypical (Sezary) cells or lymphadenopathy requiring haematological evaluation
Severe, treatment-resistant disease with major impact on quality of life
New or worsening photosensitivity after starting a systemic drug
reference.prognosis: Chronic actinic dermatitis tends to be persistent and can be markedly disabling, but with strict photoprotection, allergen avoidance and immunosuppressive therapy many patients improve, and slow resolution over years is possible; the actinic reticuloid variant is benign despite its lymphoma-like appearance, though it warrants careful follow-up.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the dense infiltrate of actinic reticuloid as cutaneous lymphoma and instituting inappropriate treatment
Failing to perform photopatch and patch testing and thereby missing treatable contact allergens
Underestimating the breadth of the action spectrum, so that ordinary sunscreens give inadequate protection
Overlooking a contributory photosensitising drug in an older patient on multiple medications
references: British Photodermatology Group guidance on the idiopathic photodermatoses
